name: THE SMELLS LIKE POUTINE SPIRIT BURGER

recipe.history:
Poutine is the great culinary export of Quebec, a dish whose origin is contested with the kind of regional pride that only food can inspire. Multiple establishments in the Centre-du-Québec region claim to have invented it in the late 1950s or early 1960s, with the most widely cited story placing its birth at Le Lutin qui Rit in Warwick, Quebec in 1957, where a customer named Fernand Lachance allegedly demanded that fries and cheese curds be mixed together, and Lachance responded that the result would be "a damn mess" — poutine in Québécois slang meaning roughly "a mess." The dish is strikingly simple in its canonical form: french fries, fresh cheese curds (specifically the fresh, squeaky, unaged kind that exists at a stage between fresh curd and aged cheese), and a hot brown gravy ladled over the top. The heat of the gravy partially melts the curds into something soft and stringy without fully liquefying them, and the result is a combination of textures — crisp fry, yielding curd, slick gravy — that is simultaneously humble and deeply satisfying. Poutine spread from rural Quebec into the rest of Canada through the 1970s and 1980s and arrived in the United States as a food trend in the 2000s, appearing on restaurant menus from New York to Los Angeles before settling into the broader landscape of American comfort food.

The poutine burger — placing the components of poutine directly on a beef patty — emerged from the "burger as vehicle for other foods" tradition that produced truffle fry burgers, mac and cheese burgers, and various other assemblies that treat the patty as a base for a more complex composition. Canadian burger joints pioneered the specific poutine burger format, and it crossed south with the same energy as the original dish: a natural pairing of two beef-friendly comfort foods. The gravy that works on fries is the same gravy that works on a burger; the cheese curds that squeak against fries do interesting textural things against a hot patty crust; the fries themselves add structural crunch that no lettuce leaf can replicate. The result is unapologetically excessive and completely delicious.

I ate my first poutine at three in the morning at a diner in Montreal where the clientele was evenly divided between club kids and truck drivers, both of whom were eating poutine with the same blank concentration. I was twenty-three and had been walking for six hours in February and nothing in my life up to that point had tasted as right as that specific bowl of fries, curds, and gravy at that specific moment. I have spent years trying to recapture that combination of circumstances — hunger, cold, exhaustion, three in the morning — through the cooking itself, and what I have found is that poutine on a burger gets surprisingly close. The ratios matter: more gravy than you think, fries that are genuinely crisp, curds that are fresh enough to squeak if you can find them.

The poutine burger presents a specific argument for medium rare cooking that goes beyond flavor: it is a question of structural integrity. The fries on top of this burger are crisp, the curds are soft and slightly melted, the gravy is wet and rich. A well-done patty in this environment would absorb the gravy without resistance and collapse into the other elements, losing its identity as the centerpiece of the sandwich. A medium rare patty at 130–135°F has enough internal integrity — the proteins tightened just enough, the crust sufficiently rigid — to hold its position under the weight and moisture of the poutine components. Every bite should contain a clear note of beef alongside the gravy and fries, and that only happens when the beef is cooked correctly. Medium rare is not just flavor — it is architecture.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
1 liter (4 cups) peanut or canola oil for frying
225g (8 oz) fresh white cheddar cheese curds (squeaky fresh, not aged)
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BUNS — Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in a stand mixer bowl.
2. Add warm milk, warm water, egg, and butter. Mix with dough hook on low until combined, then medium speed for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
3. Cover and let rise until doubled, about 1 hour.
4. Divide into 4 portions, shape into balls, place on a parchment-lined sheet pan, flatten. Cover and proof 45 minutes.
5. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash. Bake 16–18 minutes until golden. Cool on a wire rack.
6. MAKE THE POUTINE GRAVY — Melt butter in a saucepan over medium heat. Add shallot and garlic; cook 2 minutes until softened.
7. Whisk in flour and cook 2 minutes, stirring constantly, until the roux smells slightly nutty and turns pale golden.
8. Slowly whisk in beef broth a splash at a time at first to prevent lumps, then in a steady stream. Add Worcestershire and soy sauce.
9. Bring to a simmer, whisking frequently, and cook 8–10 minutes until the gravy is smooth and coats a spoon generously. Season with black pepper and salt. Keep warm over low heat.
10. MAKE THE FRIES — Cut potatoes into ¼-inch sticks. Soak in cold water for at least 30 minutes. Drain and dry thoroughly on kitchen towels.
11. Heat oil to 325°F (163°C) in a heavy pot. Fry potatoes in batches for 4–5 minutes until cooked through but pale. Drain on a wire rack. Let cool completely.
12. Heat oil to 375°F (190°C). Fry potatoes again in batches until golden and very crisp, 2–3 minutes. Drain immediately, season with salt, and keep warm in a 200°F oven on a rack.

13. FORM THE PATTIES — Divide beef into 4 equal portions (about 170g each). Form into patties ¾-inch thick with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and garlic powder just before cooking.
14. COOK THE PATTIES — Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat with a thin film of neutral oil until smoking.
15. Cook patties undisturbed for 3 minutes until a deep brown crust forms. Flip once.
16. Cook 2–2½ more minutes. Check internal temperature — target 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare.
17. Remove and tent with foil. Rest 3 minutes.
18. TOAST THE BUNS — Split buns and toast cut-side down in the pan over medium heat, 60–90 seconds.
19. ASSEMBLE — Place the patty on the bottom bun.
20. Scatter a generous handful of cheese curds over the hot patty — the heat will begin to soften them.
21. Immediately ladle hot gravy generously over the curds and patty.
22. Pile a handful of fresh hot fries directly on top of the gravy-soaked curds.
23. Scatter sliced scallions over the fries.
24. Cap with the top bun — press gently to compress slightly. Serve immediately and eat fast.
